1qvkhf1: Celebrating is a huge part of social life in Spanish. To take part you need three things: clear **dates**, **phrases** for inviting and replying, and a good **excuse** for when you can't go.
zqs02: In Spanish the date goes in this order: **el + number + de + month**: **el 21 de octubre**, **el 3 de mayo**. If you add the year: **el 3 de mayo de 2027** (_dos mil veintisiete_). If you add the day of the week, it goes first: **el sábado 17 de octubre**.
6yrnzx: To ask: **¿Qué día es hoy?** → **Hoy es lunes, 12 de octubre.** **¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños?** → **Es el 9 de julio.** In Spain you also hear **¿A cuántos estamos?** → **Estamos a 12.**
1lakbit: The 1st: in Latin America people almost always say **el primero de mayo**; in Spain **el uno de mayo** is very normal. Both are understood everywhere. The other days use normal numbers: _el dos, el tres, el veinte…_
trc3d: Months are written in **lowercase**: _enero, julio, diciembre_. And when we write the date with numbers, the day comes **first**: **9/7** is the 9th of July, not the 7th of September.
1gzi0vy: With months alone we use **en**: **Mi cumpleaños es en julio.** With a specific date we use **el**: **Mi cumpleaños es el 9 de julio.**
ub73jj: *Seasons depend on the hemisphere: in Argentina or Chile, December is summer. In Panama, near the equator, people talk more about **la temporada seca** (the dry season, roughly December to April) and **la temporada de lluvias** (the rainy season).
5yf9p9: With a specific date, only **el**. _En_ goes with the month alone: _en abril_.
1679h8p: The ordinals you learned for floors also work for the calendar: **la primera semana de agosto**, **el segundo fin de semana de mayo**, **el tercer domingo de junio**.
17fgc9i: Remember: **primer** and **tercer** before a masculine noun (_el primer día_, _el tercer domingo_), and **primera, tercera** with a feminine one (_la primera semana_).
5pcwbd: Many holidays have a fixed date (_Navidad es el 25 de diciembre_) and others change every year: _el Día de la Madre es el segundo domingo de mayo_ in many countries, but not in all.
hsnkmb: For the day of the month we use the normal number. Only the 1st can be _primero_.
1wdq1qf: **¿Por qué?** (two words, with an accent mark) asks the reason: **¿Por qué estás tan contenta?** **Porque** (one word, no accent mark) gives the reason: **Porque mañana es mi cumpleaños.**
1bp5vdt: **Es que…** also explains, but it has another use: presenting an **excuse** or justifying yourself gently. It is the most natural way to say no to an invitation: **—¿Vienes a la cena? —Ay, lo siento, es que tengo que trabajar.**
eqepq5: Why isn't _porque_ enough? Compare: **No voy porque no quiero** (direct, it can sound harsh) and **Lo siento, es que tengo mucho trabajo** (kind). With _es que_ the other person understands that you would like to go.
11cslt2: **¿Por qué no…?** is also used to suggest: **¿Por qué no hacemos una fiesta sorpresa?**
1ygj65n: In the question they are **two words with an accent mark**: _por qué_.
19s23l2: To give the reason: **porque**, one word, no accent mark.
18v0w81: _Porque no_ sounds very dry. With **es que** and _lo siento_, the refusal is kind.
2ok6jx: **Inviting.** The simplest way is a question with _querer_: **¿Quieres venir a mi fiesta?** Also: **¿Vienes a cenar el sábado?**, **Te invito a mi cumpleaños**. In Spain you often hear **¿Te apetece…?**; in many Latin American countries, **¿Te animas a…?**. With vos: **¿Querés venir?**
giow4d: **Accepting with enthusiasm.** **¡Claro! ¡Qué buena idea! ¡Me encanta! ¡Genial!** And a very useful question: **¿Llevo algo?**
1r4k1pm: **Declining kindly.** Follow four steps: thank → regret → explain with _es que_ → suggest something else. **Gracias por la invitación. ¡Qué pena! Es que ese día tengo que trabajar. ¿Quedamos otro día?**

11v44nz: In week 4 you saw that the yes-or-no question **rises** at the end and the statement **falls**. The exclamation is a third melody: it **starts high**, puts a lot of force on the important word, and **falls** clearly at the end: **¡Qué sorpresa!**, **¡Felicidades!**, **¡Es tu cumpleaños!**
1fi30bi: Compare three sentences with the same words: _Es tu cumpleaños._ (information, medium tone, falls) · _¿Es tu cumpleaños?_ (question, rises at the end) · _¡Es tu cumpleaños!_ (surprise or joy: higher, more energy, falls at the end).
sjlfuo: In exclamations with **qué** (_¡Qué bonito!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Qué buena idea!_), _qué_ and the stressed syllable of the adjective are the two peaks. Don't say them in a flat tone: in Spanish, an exclamation without energy sounds boring or ironic.
ohyfk7: In a **list**, each item ends a bit high, as if saying "there's more"; only the **last** one, after _y_, falls: _Hay música ↗, comida ↗, bebidas ↗ y un pastel ↘._ If you fall earlier, the other person thinks the list is over.
1vosu60: The melody changes by country: in the Río de la Plata the stressed syllable is stretched a lot; in the Caribbean, also in Panama, the voice rises and falls with more movement. But the basic pattern (high energy and a falling end) is understood everywhere.
9yqixp: In Spanish the exclamation is written with two marks: **¡** at the beginning and **!** at the end. The opening one warns the reader from the first word which melody to use. Exclamatory **qué** takes an accent mark: _¡Qué bonito!_
